cards.title: What is a Virtual Environment?
cards.content:
A Python virtual environment is an isolated space where you can install specific versions of Python packages without affecting your global Python installation or other projects.

It creates a folder containing a copy of the Python interpreter and all necessary site-packages.

content.question: What is the primary benefit of using a Python virtual environment?

options.text: It makes your Python code execute faster.
It isolates project dependencies to prevent version conflicts.
It automatically converts Python 2 code to Python 3.
It compiles Python code into native machine binaries.

cards.title: Creating a Virtual Environment
cards.content:
To create a virtual environment, navigate to your project directory in the terminal and run the built-in venv module:

python -m venv venv

This will generate a new folder named venv containing the isolated Python environment.

content.text: To create a virtual environment using the built-in module, you run: python -m ___ myenv

cards.title: Activating the Environment
cards.content:
Before you can use the virtual environment, you must activate it:

  • Windows (Command Prompt): venv\Scripts\activate.bat
  • Windows (PowerShell): venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
  • macOS / Linux: source venv/bin/activate

cards.title: Managing Packages with Pip
cards.content:
Once activated, any package you install via pip goes exclusively into this virtual environment.

pip install requests
pip freeze > requirements.txt

The requirements.txt file is used to list all dependencies so they can be easily reinstalled later.

cards.title: Deactivation and Cleanup
cards.content:
When you are done working on your project, you can leave the virtual environment by simply typing:

deactivate

This returns your terminal session to the global Python environment.
